name: Deosai National Park
blurb: High plateau of sedge meadows, marmots and a small brown bear population.

tip.title: Remove the marmots
tip.text: Marmots are prey for wolves, snow leopards, eagles and bears. Set Himalayan marmot to -100% and watch those predators and the vulture that scavenges.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Soil microbes and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead sedges, dung and carcasses on the cold plateau and return nutrients to the thin soil.
A colonial burrower of alpine grassland that eats grasses and flowering herbs and hibernates for about seven months. Prey for many predators.
A mountain goat of rocky slopes that eats mainly grasses and sedges in summer. Wolves, snow leopards and brown bears hunt it.
The most recorded bird near the plateau, a ground-nesting songbird of open country that eats seeds and small insects.
A critically endangered omnivore that eats grasses, roots, berries, insects and small mammals. Deosai holds its most stable population.
A small weasel that hunts rodents and ground birds; GloBI records it eating horned larks.
A small falcon that hovers over open ground to take rodents and small birds; GloBI records it eating horned larks.
A scavenger that lives mostly on bone and carrion from hoofed animals, and sometimes takes small live prey such as marmots.
A high-altitude wolf that takes marmots and wild goats and sheep where they live.
An elusive mountain cat that preys on ibex and marmots on the high slopes.
A large eagle that hunts marmots and other animals across open ground, and takes young ibex.

story: Deosai National Park protects 843 square kilometres of high-elevation alpine plain in Pakistan. Situated at an average elevation of 4,114 metres above sea level, it is the second highest plateau in the world. The park is home to rich flora and fauna of the Karakoram-West Tibetan Plateau alpine steppe eco-region.
matters: The national park was established to protect the survival of the critically endangered Himalayan brown bear and its habitat. The plateau is currently home to the most significant and stable Himalayan brown bear population.
